title: 4 Days Minimalistic Upper body Dominant PPL (Push x2) program review
summary: NH reviews a viewer's 4-day push/pull/push/legs minimalist program and largely approves it. He moves the deadlift to pull day as the opener and barbell rows to leg day with higher reps, suggests supersets and a second push-day variation, and lists missing work such as calves, rear delts, biceps and long-head triceps.
claims: Minimalism can be effective when properly put into action
The standard push/pull/legs template is the worst of the three PPL templates because legs get two sessions for every upper-body session
Your lower body already moves much more tonnage than your upper body, so a leg-heavy PPL can create imbalances; doing push twice balances it
3x5 is one of NH's favorite static rep ranges, especially for bench, though an evolving rep range can improve it
A strength lift like the rack pull can go at the end of a session if the earlier work does not re-tax its muscles, so you are fresh for it
Order the movements you want to progress on first: you are freshest and less likely to skip early sets
A 3x5 overhead press can plateau as a middle ground between volume and intensity; try more sets or reps, and introduce evolving rep ranges there first rather than on the bench
Keep a static rep scheme on the day's only horizontal press for steady tonnage progression, because evolving rep ranges make tonnage harder to manage
Once you are past a certain level, do unweighted bodyweight movements like dips for as many reps as possible rather than within a rep range
Superset to save time: incline dumbbell press with neck curls, dips with overhead triceps extensions, or a giant set of dips, extensions and neck curls
When a push day is repeated twice a week, create two versions with the same movements but different rep ranges, order or variations to avoid overuse injuries and plateaus
Start pull day with deadlifts rather than barbell rows; it improves the synergy of the whole day
Heavy barbell rows before weighted chin-ups pre-fatigue the lats, biceps and forearms and sandbag the chin-ups
The barbell row resembles a pull from the floor and involves the posterior chain heavily, which is why some say it is not the best for the upper back
Deadlift 1x5 followed by weighted chin-ups 3x5-8 is a good strength pairing on pull day
Kroc rows done to target the upper back can be supersetted with cable rows, which become a stretch- and technique-focused horizontal pull
Shrugs in a hip-hinge position target the mid and lower traps; rows with a vertical torso are effectively shrugs
Superset shrugs with hammer curls; there is no point resting after shrugs
Some people feel neck work supersetted with Kroc rows or shrugs weakens their neck-trap connection, others feel better; try it
Do pump curls with an elastic band instead of dumbbells for injury prevention, a good biceps stretch and an excellent pump
Barbell rows at 3x5 are too low; you will pull with your legs. Use 3x6-10 instead
Doing rows after squats on leg day means the posterior chain is warm but fresh enough since no hip hinge was done yet
On leg day, finish with hanging leg raises to decompress the spine
Leg day need not be lower-body only; train weak upper-body parts there too
Organize a 4-day push/pull/push/legs as push, pull, rest, push, legs according to your recovery
Leg minimalism works as long as you squat and deadlift with smart rep ranges and never get injured; legs will keep growing
Add biceps volume by doing chin-ups on push day, with a neutral grip if they interfere with weighted chin-ups
Add long-head triceps work with a band in a nucleus-overload style for growth and injury prevention
exercises: 3x5; consider evolving rep range if stalled
3x10-12, elbows flared for upper back; superset with cable rows
superset with Kroc rows; focus on stretch and technique
pump work instead of light dumbbell curls
3x5 too low, leads to using legs
